body:
There are two inputs here and no third. The objection slot is empty, so nothing in what I was given is a criticism aimed at either the account or the rival; the tension worth working is between them. I don't treat the empty slot as evidence that either survives unmoved — it only means I'm arguing with the material actually present.

The rival's central move is the one I want to keep: it reframes the account's diagnosis as one reading among at least three, and shows that the account's remedy — write it down, check in weekly, approach the avoidant friend — is a response to the first reading specifically. That is a real limit on the account, not a quibble. The material states recurring arguments, later disagreement about what an agreement meant, changing schedules, and an avoidance. It does not state load imbalance, escalation, or whether the avoidance is new in kind. So the memory-gap reading is underdetermined and should be carried as a hypothesis, not a finding — which the account itself half-concedes when it calls its work a reading rather than a diagnosis.

Where I revise the rival: its probe — ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant — is worth doing, but not on the terms the rival gives it. The rival treats the answers as discriminating between scope, recurrence, and timing, while also conceding that recollection is exactly what is in dispute. So the probe cannot recover what was actually agreed, only what each person now reports. That is still informative: clustering on one dimension points at a narrower fix than a whole new system. The probe should be read as a report about present reconstruction, not testimony about a past agreement, and a non-clustering result should count against the recording hypothesis rather than be reinterpreted as support. I would also make it forward-looking as well as backward-looking — asking what each person expects of the coming week, since what is changing is schedules.

Where I revise the account: the rival's point that a written record is not self-interpreting is the most useful single thing in either input. "A: dishes, Mon" does not say whether dishes recur, what counts as dishes, or whether it was a role or a one-off. That does not kill the record; it changes its design. The record has to be paired with an explicit scope statement at the moment of agreement — when I say I'll do the dishes this week, I mean these specific tasks, this week, and then we re-agree. With that pairing, the account's remedy and the rival's second reading stop being alternatives and fuse. I would put the scope statement first and the written record second, because the record's value depends on the scope statement doing its work.

On the avoidant friend: I accept the rival's reframing — approach to hear their view of the group conversations, not to ask why they avoid — but I hold it more loosely than the rival does. Even that framing presumes the conversations are what the avoidance is about; the avoidance might predate the chores or be about something else entirely. The rival's own warning cuts at the reframed version too: a one-to-one talk about the group conversations can still position the person as the subject of a private discussion. So I do not think one-to-one first is clearly right. The account's weaker claim — that avoidance is a symptom worth understanding before it is treated as a problem to correct — I do accept.

What I would actually do, offered as a direction rather than a validated remedy: state scope aloud at the moment of agreement; do one listening pass with each flatmate separately, framed as wanting their view; hold the written record in reserve until the probe shows where disagreements cluster. If they cluster on scope, the fix is a definition; on recurrence, a cadence; on timing, a schedule. If they do not cluster, the record is likely to relocate the argument rather than settle it, and the standing-negotiation reading the rival raises gains weight.

What remains unresolved and I won't paper over: whether one person bears a disproportionate load; whether the arguments are doing work other than failing to agree, and whether the absence of a record is load-bearing rather than accidental; whether the household wants anything formalized; whether the avoidance is recent or long-standing. I also don't know whether all three can talk without a mediator, which the avoidance itself puts in question. A mediator, a different division of labor, or naming the avoidance rather than the chores as the problem could all be better than what I have sketched, and nothing in the material ranks them.

If this is continued, I would take up a low-cost first test: the scope-statement practice plus the shaped probe, watching specifically whether "what was agreed" disputes fall and whether the reports cluster — and report what the household actually says rather than what fits the account's conjecture or the rival's three readings.
commitments:
Taking this up commits me to carrying the diagnosis as a set of live hypotheses rather than settling on the memory-gap reading. That is a claim about what the material shows — underdetermination — not a claim about what is happening in the flat. The commitment is falsifiable cheaply: if disagreements cluster on one dimension (scope, recurrence, or timing), the memory-gap reading narrows rather than dies; if they do not cluster at all, it weakens and the standing-negotiation reading gains.

I am committing to one specific design revision and taking it as mine, while crediting it to the rival's second reading: a written record must be paired with an explicit scope statement at the moment of agreement, and the scope statement should come first. If the record is adopted without that pairing, I would expect it to relocate the disagreement rather than settle it. I flag this as the part of my contribution most likely to be wrong if the flat's real friction turns out to be about something other than meaning.

The shaped probe is an application-type commitment, not a validated method. Its relevance is that the pattern of answers discriminates between readings; its weakness, inherited from the rival and not fully repaired by me, is that recollection is what is already in dispute, so the answers are reports rather than testimony. Anyone taking it up should be prepared for it to return nothing decisive, and should not treat non-clustering as support for whichever reading they already favored.

The approach to the avoidant friend is the move I would most expect to be contested, and I hold it more loosely than either the account or the rival proposes. I am criticizing the account for presenting one-to-one first as clearly right; I am not claiming the rival's reframing fixes that. The framing "I want to hear your view of the group conversations" still presumes the conversations are the issue, and it can still single the person out. The grounds for the approach should be curiosity about their experience, and if it produces more avoidance, that should count against my framing rather than be explained away as resistance.

There is an unresolved problem I cannot close: the rival argues the absence of a record may be load-bearing — that a record would move the argument onto the record rather than settle it. I have not shown a record makes things worse, nor have I proposed a full alternative. Whether relocation is an improvement or a delay is not something the material decides.

I am not committing to: that the account is wrong, that the problem is really about status, that the avoidant friend is outnumbered, or that any particular chore is neglected. Those would be inventions. I also note that the objection slot was empty; I am not treating that as a verdict on either the account or the rival.

What I propose to take up: the low-cost first test — scope-statement practice plus the shaped probe — and a specific watch, whether "what was agreed" disputes fall and whether the reports cluster. That commitment is to further inquiry and to reporting what the flatmates say, not to the truth of the reading.
